What is Cubeon Launcher?

Cubeon Launcher, also called Cubeon Minecraft Launcher, is a free, open-source desktop app for Minecraft Java Edition on Windows and Linux. This is the official Cubeon website. Install game versions, manage modded instances, customize skins and cosmetics, and play with friends.
About Cubeon and official project links explains the platforms, license and local player profiles. Cubeon is a separate project from the similarly named Cubion launcher.

Looking for the best Minecraft launcher for your setup? Start with your game edition, server account requirements and mod loader. Our guide explains where Cubeon fits, what to check before downloading, and how to assess FPS claims.

Install the Minecraft launcher, add mods, resource packs and shaders, or set up a modpack. Use the guides to play Minecraft with friends and troubleshoot a crash. The official Cubeon source repository and release history are on GitHub.

Any name, three to sixteen characters. No email, no password.

Cubeon is a good fit if you want a free, open-source Java Edition launcher with compatible mod loaders, mods, modpacks, skins and friends on Windows or Linux. Add friends by their Cubeon name and the launcher keeps the conversation, showing who's online and what they're playing. Can I bring my own mods or modpacks?{0}

Yes. Open Settings, go to Import, and point it at the folder your mods live in. Cubeon lists everything it finds - mods, resource packs, shader packs, modpacks and worlds - and installs what you pick for the version you chose.
What does my computer need?{0}

Where are my name and skins kept, and who sees them?{0}

On your computer, in the .cubeon_launcher folder inside your user folder. Your skin and cape are shared so other Cubeon players see them when you play together. Change or remove them whenever you like.
Will you email me?{0}

What is Cubeon?

Cubeon Launcher, also called Cubeon Minecraft Launcher, is a free, open-source desktop launcher for Minecraft Java Edition. It manages game versions, modded instances, mods, modpacks, skins, cosmetics, friends and local servers in one app.

This is the official Cubeon website, www.ylet.online. The official source repository is Shadow-457/Cubeon on GitHub. Cubeon is a separate project from the similarly named Cubion launcher. Use these official links to identify Cubeon when looking for downloads or support.
Project facts
Product: Cubeon Launcher, a desktop app for Minecraft Java Edition.
Platforms: Windows 10 and 11 and Linux. macOS is untested and downloads are unavailable.
Price: the launcher is free.
Source license: Apache License 2.0. Bundled third-party components keep their own licenses.
Source code: Python and Flet for the desktop launcher, Java for the companion Minecraft client.
Player profiles: local/offline names; Cubeon does not provide Microsoft account sign-in.
Game edition: Minecraft Java Edition. Cubeon does not launch Bedrock Edition.
Downloads and releases

Use the official download page for platform options or the latest stable GitHub release for its files and release notes. Windows uses the Setup.exe installer. Linux has an AppImage, a setup installer and a Debian/Ubuntu package. macOS is untested and downloads are unavailable.

All releases also includes versions marked as prereleases for beta testing. Check the release label before downloading. Packaged builds do not require Python; source setup instructions are in the repository.
Mods, profiles and playing together

Cubeon supports Vanilla, Fabric, Quilt, Forge and NeoForge configurations. A mod must match the Minecraft version and loader of the instance you launch. Vanilla accepts resource packs, while mods and shaders need a compatible modded setup.

The launcher browses mods through Modrinth, manages modpacks, and lets you import local content. The mods and shaders guide explains compatibility and dependencies; the modpacks guide covers packs and imports.

Friends features include launcher chat and presence. Local player profiles cannot join servers that require Microsoft authentication. Read the multiplayer profile limitations before choosing a server.
Skins, capes, shoulder companions and back cosmetics are documented in the cosmetics guide. In-game feature support depends on the game version, loader and companion client.

Home / Benchmarks
Benchmarks
Cubeon against two other launchers on the same PC, the same Minecraft version, frame by frame from screen recordings - and the caveats written down next to the numbers.
Measured 15 October 2026 · Minecraft 1.21.11 · Xeon E5-1650, Radeon RX 580
The short version
Fastest in game, and the steadiest when it dips

Three one-minute runs per launcher, one FPS sample for every second of video. In game, Cubeon averaged 206 FPS - about 35% above FastClient and 74% above SKLauncher. Its worst single second was 102 FPS; the other two dropped to 37 and 33.
206 FPS average in game
The highest of the three, and the highest average across the whole recording (233 FPS).
102 FPS lowest second
The gap that matters most: FastClient bottomed out at 37 FPS and SKLauncher at 33.
+35% over FastClient
152 FPS average in game - a performance-focused launcher, measured on the same machine.
+74% over SKLauncher
119 FPS average in game. It also ran with no mods at all - see the caveats below.
How it was measured
Read from the video, not from a built-in counter

Each launcher was recorded playing Minecraft 1.21.11 on the same PC, in three separate one-minute runs. The frame rate was then counted frame by frame out of the screen recordings - one sample per second of video - rather than trusting each launcher's own FPS display. "In game" means roughly 28-32 seconds of actual gameplay per launcher; "menu" is the pause screen.
All three launched as-is

Nothing was added or changed by hand for any of them. On the SKLauncher side there was no Sodium and no mods at all - plain vanilla - so it is being compared against launchers that ship Sodium. That is the honest reading of its numbers: a big part of the gap is the performance mods Cubeon installs for you, not the launcher's own code.

Cubeon's FPS boost is on by default, and it is the reason Cubeon ships Sodium. The switch installs Sodium plus five companion mods (Lithium, ImmediatelyFast, Entity Culling, FerriteCore and More Culling) into the profile you launch, and sets the graphics options that cost frames to their fast values. Turn it off and the next launch restores vanilla graphics - the switch is in the Play menu, and it says which way it is set.

What the numbers mean
Cubeon was fastest in game - about 206 FPS on average, roughly 35% above FastClient (152) and 74% above SKLauncher (119).
Cubeon also had the best worst case. Its lowest in-game second was 102 FPS, against 37 (FastClient) and 33 (SKLauncher). The average is the headline; this is the one you feel.
FastClient held up best between menu and game - only about an 8% drop, where Cubeon and SKLauncher each lost about 19%. It is the most consistent of the three, just not the fastest.
SKLauncher looked frame-capped on the pause menu at about 147 FPS, and was the slowest in game with the deepest dips.
Read it honestly
What this test is not
A comparison like this is easy to make flattering. Here is everything that weakens it, in the order it matters.

Not a lab test. Each launcher was recorded in a different spot in the world, so the comparison is indicative rather than controlled. The same world, the same camera path and several runs per launcher would be a stronger test.
F3 was on for Cubeon and SKLauncher, off for FastClient (it uses its own FPS display). The debug screen costs a little FPS, so this slightly favours FastClient - and the gap is still large.

Nothing was equalised. SKLauncher ran vanilla with no Sodium and no mods, and its own defaults differed (fancy clouds, RGSS filtering, where Cubeon was on fast clouds with no filtering). Its numbers say "a vanilla install on this PC", not "this launcher's best".
FastClient's digits are blurry in the video. A few of its menu readings may be off by about 5 FPS. Every reading was checked by eye, twice.
What we would like to do next

Run all three with identical settings, the same world and the same camera path, several times each, and publish that alongside this. If you want to help with a recording on your own hardware, the Discord is the place - more machines make this more useful.

Why there's no banner

Cubeon has no advertising trackers and sets no tracking cookies. Page views are counted by Vercel Web Analytics, which is cookieless: it writes nothing to your device, so there is no cookie to ask you about. For each view it records the page, the referring site, your browser, operating system and device type, a rough location and the time, and keeps them only as aggregate totals. Visitors are told apart with a one-way hash of the request that is discarded after 24 hours - no identifier that follows you between sites or between days.

Fonts and pictures come from this site. The shared download count uses our download server. Uploading a Doctor log or choosing Analyze log sends a redacted excerpt to our Kilo endpoint; on-device checks run in your browser. See Privacy - page counts.
The download counter

The download buttons keep a shared count of how many different people have downloaded - the same total for everyone, and one per visitor rather than one per click. Our download server records a one-way hash of the address the request already carries, only so the same visitor is not counted twice; the address itself is not stored, and the hash is not linked to any account, cookie or profile. If that request can't be made, the count simply doesn't appear.
Optional Doctor AI

Doctor does not load an AI provider script, create a visitor account or use provider sign-in cookies. Uploading a file or choosing Analyze log sends the excerpt to Cubeon's server, which calls Kilo auto/free. Local checks and file previews work without it. Logs and guides are kept in page memory, not Cubeon browser storage. See Doctor privacy details.
Small interface preferences
Cubeon Bench is coming soon. Projects and preferences saved with its previous editor may remain in this browser. Its coming-soon page uses the same cookieless Vercel page counts as the main website.

The dismissal of our cookie information badge is remembered in localStorage on this browser. If a consent banner is enabled, its choice is also stored there. The language you pick for the site is saved as {0} so it is not asked again. These preferences are not sent to an analytics service.
What the app stores

The Cubeon launcher keeps your settings, your name and your skins in a folder on your computer. Those are ordinary files rather than cookies, and they stay on your machine unless you upload a skin so that other players can see it.
If we ever add something

If a future feature needs to store something on your device - simple anonymous counts, say - we'll ask first. A clear yes and an equally easy no, nothing switched on until you choose, nothing ticked in advance. The privacy page will say what and why.

Cosmetics
Open Cosmetics and find the Your Skins section.
Upload a skin file. It must be a PNG in the standard Minecraft layout: 64×64, or the older 64×32 format.
The 3D preview updates with the real pixels from your file. Drag it to turn the model around before you commit.
Pick Use on the card to make it active. Everything you upload stays in your library, so switching back is one click.

Cubeon reads the arm width from the image, so a slim (Alex-style) skin renders with slim arms without you choosing a model. A skin exported in the wrong model looks stretched rather than broken - that is a re-export, not a launcher fault.
Choosing None puts you back on Minecraft's own default model. That is a normal choice, not a failure: the preview shows Steve or Alex because that is exactly what the game will show.
This is the part that causes most "my skin is broken" messages, so it is worth being precise:

You, in game. Minecraft cannot fetch a skin for an offline name, so Cubeon installs a skin loader into the instance you launch. That is what makes your own skin appear. It needs a modded instance - vanilla cannot load it.
Other Cubeon players. Your skin is also published to Cubeon's skin service, and Cubeon's client reads it from there. Two Cubeon players with skin support see each other's skins.

Everyone else. A player on vanilla, on another launcher, or on a server that overrides skins sees the default model. There is no way around this: it is the price of playing without a Microsoft account.
Your cape is served to every Cubeon player, which is why the launcher describes it as the part other people see. See Capes.
First launch after uploading
Skin support is installed the next time you press Play on a modded instance. If the upload is minutes old and the game was already open, close the game and start it again.
Capes live in the same place as skins, in their own section. Upload a cape PNG (the standard cape layout) and pick it the same way.
With nothing selected you wear the default Cubeon cape, so you are not left blank.
None hides the cape entirely - including the default one. That is deliberate, and it is the only way to truly remove it.
Capes are visible to other Cubeon players. Like skins, they are invisible to a vanilla client.

Home / Docs / Files & backups
Two folders in your user folder hold everything Cubeon knows: one for the launcher, one for the game. Once you know which is which, deleting the safe things becomes obvious.
Mods and content folders
The map
{0} means your home folder. On Windows that is {1} - the folder with your name on it, not {2}.
Folder
What is in it
The launcher itself: settings, your local identity, caches, downloaded Java runtimes, your skin and cape files, and the launcher log.
The game: installed versions, instances, mods, resource packs, shaders, worlds, screenshots and crash reports.
Both are yours. Nothing in them needs an installer, and copying them to another machine carries everything across - see moving to a new PC.
Cubeon keeps its game files private

It uses its own {0} folder rather than the standard {1} one on purpose: another launcher updating or cleaning its files cannot then wipe a version Cubeon is using, and Cubeon cannot change what another launcher reads.
Every instance plays in its own folder:
These are real, separate copies per instance:
{0} - your worlds
{0} - mod configs
{0} - video settings, keybinds, language
{0} - your server list
These are shared with every other instance, and appear in the folder as links to one copy:
{0} - the skin setup

So: changing a video setting in one instance does not change it in another, but installing a mod applies everywhere. That is the intended split - a world should be private, a mod library should not be downloaded twice.
Deleting an instance does not delete its {0} folder. If the world matters, copy that folder out first.
Two layers, and it helps to know which is which before you drag a jar anywhere:
{0}, {1}, {2} - what the game reads right now. Cubeon rebuilds these at launch from the instance you selected, so treat them as a staging area.
{0} and {1} - the real library: one clearly named copy of each mod, pack and shader, shared by every instance.
A jar you drop into {0} by hand is adopted for the instance you are playing and is never deleted - it is yours, not Cubeon's. See adding a jar by hand.
If Cubeon has to move a jar out of the way, it puts it in {0} rather than destroying it. Files a modpack replaces are backed up under {1} with a timestamp.
File
What it tells you
The launcher's own log: startup, downloads, installs and launcher errors. Send this one when the app itself misbehaves.
Minecraft's crash reports, one file per crash. Send the newest one when the game crashes.
Minecraft's normal game log, including the {0} from the last run. Useful when the game closed without a crash report.

Before sending anything, open it in a text editor and remove what you would not post publicly: your name, your home folder path, private server addresses, and anything that looks like a key or token. The Crash Doctor also redacts an excerpt for you, but it says plainly that automatic redaction cannot catch everything.
Which one to send: launcher closed on its own → {0}. Game crashed → the newest file in {1}. Game closed with no message → {2}.
Launcher backups

Settings > Backups saves your launcher configuration and keeps a history you can restore from. It is the safety net for settings - RAM, Java path, language, cosmetic choices - and it means a bad change costs one button, not a reinstall.
World backups are yours to make
Cubeon does not copy your worlds on a schedule. A world lives in one folder; back it up by copying that folder somewhere else while the game is closed:
Copy the whole world folder, not just {0}. To restore, close the game and put the folder back into {1}.
Mods and packs
You do not need to back these up to keep them - they are re-downloadable and the global libraries hold one copy already. Back up a hand-edited config if you spent time on it.
Close Cubeon completely, and close Minecraft.
Copy {0} and {1} to the same paths on the new machine.
Install Cubeon there and open it.
Check Settings > Java: a saved path to a Java that only existed on the old PC will not work. Clear it and let Cubeon manage Java again.
Your Cubeon name travels with {0}, which is what keeps friends, skins and servers recognising you. Keep that folder private - it is identity, not just settings.
Before you copy, know that {0} (downloaded Java) and caches are the bulky parts. Skipping them is safe: Cubeon downloads what it needs again.
Uninstalling the app and deleting your data are two different things, and only one of them is what you usually want.
Uninstall the app - removes the program. Your settings, name, worlds and mods stay exactly where they are, ready for the next install.
Delete {0} - forgets your name, skins, capes, settings and caches. This is the "start completely fresh" button, and friends will no longer recognise the old name as you.
Delete {0} - removes installed versions, worlds, mods and packs. Everything in it can be re-downloaded except your worlds, so copy {1} out first.

Never delete either folder while Cubeon or Minecraft is running: the app will write files back into the half-deleted folder, and that is how settings get corrupted. Close everything first, then delete.
If you only want to fix something, you rarely need either. Troubleshooting starts with the cheap checks, and Settings > Java plus Check & repair fix most of what a reset would.

Home / Docs / Getting started
One download, one name, one Play button. This page covers the file to pick, what happens on the first run, and the handful of settings that are worth knowing about.
Versions and loaders
Instances
Settings worth knowing
Step one
Everything is on the download page, and every build is free with no account attached. Pick the file that matches your computer:
Windows - setup file. Double-click it, click through the installer, and launch Cubeon from the Start menu. This is the easiest option for most people.

Linux - installer or package. The setup includes the launcher and icon, adds an app menu entry, and supports systems without FUSE. Debian and Ubuntu users can choose the package. The standalone AppImage remains available as an alternative.
There is no Mac build yet. When there is one, it will be on the download page.
What the computer needs
Windows 10 or 11, or a modern 64-bit Linux.
At least 4 GB of system memory for vanilla Minecraft; 8 GB or more is comfortable once you add mods.
A graphics card that can already run Minecraft, and a little disk space per installed version.
You do not need a Minecraft account, an email address, Java, or Python. Cubeon is a self-contained app, and it fetches the game files and a Java runtime itself.
If Windows warns you about the file

Small independent apps are not signed by a big publisher, so Windows SmartScreen shows a warning the first time. Choose More info, then Run anyway (or Keep if your browser asks first). Only do that for a file you downloaded from the download page - and never turn off Windows security as a whole to get an app running.
Cubeon opens on the Play tab. Three things happen, in this order:
Pick a name. Three to sixteen characters, no password, no email. The name is how friends find you, and names are first come, first served - so pick the one you want now rather than later.
Choose a Minecraft version from the version picker. Leave the loader on Vanilla unless you already know you need mods.

Press Play. The first launch downloads the game itself, so it takes a few minutes depending on your connection. A progress bar shows what is being fetched, and the button turns into Cancel while it works.
Cancelling during that first download is safe: nothing is half-installed, and pressing Play again picks up where it stopped.
Cubeon uses an offline profile

There is no Microsoft or Mojang sign-in. That is what makes "pick a name and play" possible, but it also means servers that require a real Minecraft account will reject you - see offline names and premium servers.
A "version" in Cubeon is a Minecraft release plus, optionally, a mod loader. The launcher can install these loaders for you:
Vanilla - the plain game. Resource packs work; mods and shaders do not.
Fabric and Quilt - the usual choice for performance mods, cosmetic mods and most modern packs.
Forge and NeoForge - needed by the mods and older packs that were built for them.

The important rule: a mod only runs on the loader and the Minecraft version it was built for. A Fabric mod does not work because a Forge version is installed, and a 1.20.1 mod does not work on 1.21. The mods guide starts with that check for a reason.
Install as many versions as you like. Each one is downloaded once and then starts quickly.

An instance is one version in its own folder with its own settings. Your worlds, video settings, keybinds and server list belong to the instance you launch - a redstone test world and a shader-heavy world can live side by side without fighting over {0}.
Play card - shows the instance you have selected and its loader. Folder, Rename and Delete live here.
The pencil - opens the icon picker: 20 blocks and 20 mob heads. The icon is saved per instance; clicking the card still selects it.
Shared content - installed mods, resource packs and shaders are kept once and shared by every instance, so a mod you add does not have to be added twice.
Deleting an instance does not delete its world folder. If you want the world gone too, remove that folder yourself - inside an instance shows where it is.
Java is handled for you

Cubeon uses a Java it finds on your computer when that Java is new enough for the version you picked, and otherwise downloads a free one for you. You only need to touch this if you want a specific Java build.

In that case open Settings > Java and point it at the {0} executable. Use a 64-bit build: 1.18 to 1.20.4 want Java 17, 1.20.5 and newer want Java 21, and the 26.x versions want Java 25. A path to a 32-bit Java, or to an old Java 8, is the most common reason a launch fails after someone changes this by hand.
Memory

Cubeon starts you at 4 GB, which is right for vanilla and light modding. Raise it to 6-8 GB for a heavy modpack. Going much higher on a 4 GB or 8 GB machine makes things worse, not better: the operating system and the rest of the game still need memory of their own.

In Settings > Performance > Java, expand Cubeon's default flags to see exactly what will be passed to the game, including which options were skipped on your hardware. Custom flags are added after the defaults.

FPS boost is on by default. When you launch, it installs Sodium and five companion mods (Lithium, ImmediatelyFast, Entity Culling, FerriteCore and More Culling) into that profile and sets the graphics options that cost frames to their fast values.

Turning it off restores vanilla graphics on the next launch - the switch is in the Play menu and it always says which way it is set. The benchmarks page has the measured numbers, and the caveats next to them.
Already boosted and still stuttering?
Lower your render distance first. It is almost always the single biggest setting, and it costs far less than it looks. Slow or stuttering has the rest.
Settings sit inside the account panel, in a short rail down the left. The ones people actually change:

Language - 22 languages, searchable by native name, English name or code. Arabic, Urdu, Persian and Pashto switch the whole launcher to right-to-left. A language change applies after a restart, and detailed messages without a translation fall back to English.
Custom title bar - on by default on Windows and Linux. Turn it off if your window manager draws its own title bar.
Notifications - System > Notifications > Chat messages controls incoming message alerts. Open conversations do not alert you, and old history never does.
Backups - save and restore your launcher settings and history. Backups explains what is covered.
Screenshots - its own section, with the gallery of what you have captured in game.
Import - scan an old {0} folder and pick up mods, packs and worlds from it. Packs and worlds from an old setup covers that.
Launcher updates are manual. Download a stable release or beta preview from the download page.

Run the installer for your existing Cubeon installation.
Open Cubeon after the installation finishes.
Your name, skins, worlds and installed content are not touched by an update: they live in your user folder, not in the app folder (where things live).

Home / Docs / Modpacks
A modpack is a whole game setup: its own Minecraft version, loader, mods and configs, installed in one go. Here is what that means in Cubeon.
From an old setup
Adding your own mods
Installing a pack does not sprinkle mods into your current setup. It builds a self-contained instance:
the Minecraft version the pack asks for, installed if you do not have it;
the loader the pack uses - Fabric, NeoForge, Forge or Quilt;
its mods, its configs and its overrides;
and a Play card for the pack, with its own saves, options and server list.
That isolation is the point: a 1.20.1 pack and a vanilla 1.21.4 world never share a config folder, and installing a pack cannot break a setup you already had.
Expect the download to be large. A pack plus its Minecraft version is often several hundred megabytes, so give it a few minutes on a slow connection and make sure there is room on the disk.
Open Modpacks. Browse lists packs, Installed shows what you already have.
Open a pack and read its requirements: the Minecraft version and the loader. Cubeon checks those before it starts.
Press Install and watch the progress. You can keep using the launcher; the install runs in the background and the tab tells you which step it is on.
When it finishes, the pack appears as an instance. Select it on Play and press Play.
Only one install can run at a time for the same Minecraft version and loader. Starting a second one for the same pair waits for the first rather than corrupting both.
Packs and your own worlds
A new pack starts with an empty save list. Its worlds live in the pack's own instance folder, so copy a world in only if you mean to - inside an instance shows the folder.
Cubeon reads the standard pack formats - Modrinth {0} and CurseForge packs - and it can pick things up from a Minecraft folder you already have.

Open Settings > Import, choose a folder to scan (an old {0}, a backup drive, a downloads folder), and Cubeon lists what it found: mod jars, resource and shader pack ZIPs, modpacks, and world folders (any folder with a {1}). Pick one and choose which instance to import it into.
Nothing is imported until you pick it, and anything it cannot read is counted and skipped rather than guessed at.
Install the newer version of the pack the same way you installed the first one. Cubeon:
downloads the new version's files;
puts them in place before removing anything;
then removes the jars the old version owned and the new one does not.
That order is deliberate. If the download fails halfway, you keep the pack you had - a failed update does not leave you with a half-updated, unplayable install.
Two more things it protects:
Your settings survive. Existing {0} and {1} are kept rather than overwritten. Other files the pack replaces are backed up under {2} with a timestamp.
Your own jars are not pack jars. Jars you added yourself are not part of the pack's list, so a prune does not touch them.
Your worlds are never part of an update. They live in the instance's {0} folder and stay there.
Delete the pack's instance from the Play card. Cubeon removes the version folder and the pack marker it owns.
The world folder is a separate thing and is not deleted with the instance. If you want the pack gone completely, delete its world folder too - after you have checked there is nothing in it you want.
Deleting the pack instance does not delete mods you installed yourself, and does not change your other instances.
"Install failed" is the message; the reason is in the log. The usual suspects, easiest first:
Disk space. Packs need a lot of it. Free some up and press Install again.
The network dropped. Retry - Cubeon re-checks and re-downloads rather than resuming a corrupt file.
The same version and loader are already installing. Wait for that one to finish.
The pack file itself is broken. Try another version of the pack, or install its files by hand into a blank instance (jar in {0}, configs in {1}).

If the failure happened after the pack was working, you should still have the previous version: a rebuild hides the old pack marker and restores it when the install does not finish, and old jars are pruned only after the new ones are on disk.
For the actual error text, open Cubeon Doctor with the launcher log, or ask on the Discord and paste the last few lines.
Adding your own mods to a pack
You can. It is the most common way people break a pack, so do it one mod at a time:
Add a single mod that matches the pack's Minecraft version and loader.
Launch and play for a minute. If it works, keep it; if it crashes, switch it off again.
Repeat. When something breaks, the last mod you added is the one to blame.

Two caveats worth knowing before you start: a pack update may change the mods your addition depended on, and adding a second copy of a library the pack already ships is a reliable crash. Check & repair finds the duplicate case.

Installing
Mods that don't load
The rule
Before you install anything
Two things have to match, or the mod will not load:
The Minecraft version. A mod built for 1.20.1 does not work on 1.21 - and "1.21" and "1.21.4" are different versions to Minecraft too.
The loader. Fabric mods need a Fabric instance, Forge mods need Forge, NeoForge mods need NeoForge. Vanilla cannot load mods at all.

So the first step is always: select (or create) an instance with the loader you need, on the version the mod is built for. The Mods tab uses that instance's real version and loader for its filters, which is why the download button can be unavailable for a mod you can plainly see.
Vanilla vs modded, in one line
Vanilla accepts resource packs. Mods and shaders need a modded loader, and shaders also need a shader runtime (below).
Open Mods and pick the Mods content type. The search bar shows the Minecraft version, the loader and the category it is searching in, so you can see what "compatible" means before you type anything.
The filters that matter
Compatible only - on by default. Keep it on; it is the difference between a mod that starts and a mod that crashes your game.
Search all Modrinth - a button that appears when a search comes back empty. It widens the search beyond the current version and loader, so you can confirm the mod exists at all.
All categories - if a mod seems missing, clear the category filter. Plenty of good mods are filed somewhere unexpected.
Searching by name or by link

Type a name, or paste a Modrinth project link straight into the field. A link resolves that exact project even when your filters would normally hide it - useful when a friend sends you one. Installing from it still requires a matching Minecraft version and loader, so a link is not a way around the compatibility check.
If a full name finds nothing, Cubeon retries with shorter searches and labels those results as related matches. They are worth a look, but check the version on each one before you install it.

Mods for other Minecraft versions or loaders are still shown in a project's detail view, marked as another version. Cubeon does not hide them - it just will not download one that does not fit the selected instance.
Cubeon's catalogue is Modrinth. A mod published only on another site will not appear in these results, though a jar you already have can be added by hand.
Select the instance the mod is for.
Find the mod, open it, and press Download (or Install).
Wait for the button to read Installed. The mod is now in the instance's Installed list.
Start (or restart) the game. A mod that was installed while Minecraft was open is not in that running instance of the game.

Dependencies install with it. If a mod declares that it needs Fabric API, Cloth Config or something else, Cubeon fetches the matching build of that dependency too and tells you what it added. You do not have to hunt for them - and you should not install a different version of the same dependency by hand afterwards, because two copies of one library is a classic crash.
Cubeon keeps one build per mod per launch: if two versions of the same mod are on disk, the newest mod version that fits the running instance is the one that gets loaded.
Turning a mod off
Switch it off in Installed instead of deleting it. Cubeon renames the jar rather than removing it, so switching it back on is instant and you keep the file if you want to try again.

Find the mod again and install the newer build; it replaces the old one in that instance. If a mod update breaks your game, switch the new jar off and you are back to a working setup - which is exactly why off is not the same as delete.
Removing
Remove in Installed deletes Cubeon's copy of the jar. Jars you put in the mods folder yourself are treated differently - see the next section.
Some mods are only published as a file. Put the jar in the folder the game reads for the instance you are about to launch:
On Windows that is {0}. Close Minecraft first. Cubeon rebuilds that folder at each launch from the instance you selected, so a jar you drop in is picked up for that instance and remembered as yours.
Two things Cubeon does for you here, and one it cannot:
Your jars are yours. Cubeon only removes jars it installed itself. Anything else stays where it is; if a launcher-managed change needs the space, your jar is moved to {0}, never deleted.
The build still has to be right. The jar must be for that instance's Minecraft version and loader. Cubeon cannot rewrite a mod.
Dependencies are on you. A hand-added mod does not get its dependencies resolved automatically. If it needs Fabric API, install that too.

If a launcher-managed jar is locked by another running copy of the game, Cubeon stops with a "another Minecraft window is using these mods" message instead of skipping the file. Close the other window and press Play again.

Mods > Installed has a Check & repair button. The same button exists in the installed views for resource packs and shaders. It runs Cubeon's local Doctor in the background - no dialog, no upload - and looks for:
the same mod installed twice, in two different files;
a missing required dependency;
a mod built for a different loader or Minecraft version;
conflicts the mods declare against each other;
structural problems in an installed pack.

Pressing the button authorizes reversible repairs: it can fetch missing dependencies, and it renames duplicate or incompatible jars to disabled backups rather than deleting them. Re-enable anything you want back in Installed. The result appears next to the button, and hovering it explains anything it could not resolve.
Automatic checks stay quiet

Checks at launch are limited to safe launcher settings and never wait on a question; installing content can also fetch dependencies without replacing a build you already have. Nothing gets disabled without you asking for a repair.
What it cannot do: fix a bug inside a mod, or make a mod support a Minecraft version it was not built for. Those need a different mod build, which is what the "it still doesn't load" list is for.
Resource packs work on vanilla and modded instances, but they are still version-sensitive: a pack made for 1.16 usually looks broken on 1.21.
In Mods, switch to Resource Packs and install the pack you want.
In game, open Options > Resource Packs and move it to the selected column. Cubeon does not force a pack on for you.
If a pack shows up but looks wrong (missing textures, pink blocks), it is almost always built for a different Minecraft version.
Shaders need three things at once, and the third is the one people miss:
a modded instance - Fabric or Forge family, not Vanilla;
a shader runtime for that loader, such as Iris or Oculus;
the shader pack itself, installed from the Shaders view.
Downloading a shader ZIP on its own changes nothing. Install the runtime first, then the pack, then choose it in game under Video Settings > Shader Packs.
Shaders are the most expensive thing you can turn on. If the frame rate collapses, drop the shader preset before you touch anything else.

Home / Privacy
Cubeon has no advertising or analytics profiles. Page views are counted anonymously, without cookies. Optional Doctor AI uses Groq with Kilo as a fallback; review the details below.
What Cubeon keeps
The name you pick. Three to sixteen characters, exactly what you type. It's how your friends find you.
Your skin and cape pictures, if you add them, so other Cubeon players can see them in game.

Your friends list, and the messages you send through Cubeon, so they can reach the people you're talking to. One-to-one messages are end-to-end encrypted: they're scrambled on your device and only the person you're writing to can read them. Not us.
Your IP address while you're connected. That's how the app tells a real player from a flood of fake ones, and how it stops someone taking over your name.
That's the whole list. No email address, no phone number, no real name, no date of birth, no payment details, and no Mojang or Microsoft login.
What we don't do
No advertising and no ad networks, here or in the app.

No analytics profiles and no tracking cookies. The website counts anonymous page views - see page counts - and sets no cookie to do it. Optional Doctor AI requests are described below - see Cookies. The only lasting per-visitor number the site keeps is the download counter: a shared running total of distinct visitors who downloaded. Our download server keeps a one-way hash of the address the request already carries, only so the same visitor is not counted twice; the address itself is not stored and the hash is not used for anything else.
No selling, renting or swapping your information with anybody.
No emails, so no newsletters and nothing to unsubscribe from.
No asking who you are: there's no age, name or address to hand over.
Page counts on the website

Cubeon Bench's coming-soon page uses these same anonymous page counts on this domain. Cubeon Bench is planned as a resource pack editor for Cubeon cosmetics. Previously saved editor projects remain on your device and are not sent to analytics.

The website counts page views with Vercel Web Analytics. It is cookieless: nothing is written to your device, there is no consent banner to dismiss, and no identifier is left behind for another site to read. For each view it records the page address, the site that referred you, your browser, operating system and device type, a rough location (city level) and the time. It is stored as aggregate totals, never tied to your name, your Cubeon account or your IP address.

A visitor is counted with a one-way hash built from the incoming request. That hash is discarded after 24 hours, so nothing survives that could follow you across days or across websites. There are no advertising pixels, no cross-site profiles and nothing here that could be sold.
This section covers the website only. The launcher has no analytics at all: it sends us nothing about how you use it, which mods you pick or how often you play.
Where it's kept

On your own computer, where your name, skins, settings and logs sit in a Cubeon folder in your user folder. One change at a time

Every fix here is a single change, and the rule is the same one support people use: change one thing, launch, and see. Two changes at once means you learn nothing when it works - and something confusing when it does not.
Run it from a terminal and read the error
Double-clicking hides the message that explains the failure. On Linux, start the app from a terminal so the error stays on screen. On Windows, launching {0} from Command Prompt shows the same text.
Check for a security block
Windows SmartScreen: More info → Run anyway, only for a file from the download page.
Antivirus: a fresh build can be quarantined by a scanner that has never seen it. Check the scanner's quarantine list and restore it if it is yours.
Linux AppImage: it needs to be executable. {0} it, and if the desktop still refuses, start it from a terminal to see why.
Look at the launcher log
The launcher keeps its log at:
The last few lines are the interesting ones. If the launcher is starting and dying instantly, that file usually says why. Logs explains the rest of the files in that folder.
If a settings file got damaged

Cubeon never silently replaces a readable-but-broken settings file: it copies it aside as {0} and starts from the last good copy. If you have been hand-editing files, look for one of those, and rename it back once you know what broke.
A full reinstall is the last resort, not the first: replacing the app does not change anything in {0}, which is where almost all failures live.
The launcher is fine, the game window never appears, or it flashes and closes. Check these five, in order:
Version and loader. Does the selected instance's loader exist for that Minecraft version? Reinstalling the version fixes a broken install, and takes one press.

Java. Leave Settings > Java on the managed runtime unless you have a reason. If you pointed it at your own, check it is 64-bit and the right major version: 17 for 1.18-1.20.4, 21 for 1.20.5 and newer, 25 for 26.x.
Memory. 4 GB is the default and is right for vanilla. If you set 16 GB on an 8 GB machine, Java fails to start at all - put it back.

Another game already running. Two copies of Minecraft cannot share one mods folder. Cubeon refuses with "another Minecraft window is using these mods" instead of launching a broken game. Close the other window.
Disk space. The version files, mods and worlds all need room. A full disk fails in confusing ways.
If the game starts and closes within a second, there is a crash report - the next section shows where.
When Minecraft crashes, Cubeon opens a window with the report and three buttons: Doctor, Copy log, and Discord. The report itself is also on disk, in the instance's crash folder:
You do not need to read all of it. Two lines carry almost all of the information:
Description or The game crashed whilst ... - what Minecraft was doing.
The first Caused by: line - which file or class actually failed.
The long list of {0} lines underneath is the call stack. It is useful to a developer and mostly noise to everyone else - except that a mod's name in there is a strong hint about who to blame.
Find the line that looks closest to yours. "Usually means" is doing real work in that heading - the same text can have more than one cause.
Message
Do this
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
The game ran out of allocated memory
Raise RAM one step (6 GB, then 8 GB), close other apps, lower render distance or shaders
NoClassDefFoundError / ClassNotFoundException
A required library or mod is missing, or the loader is wrong
Install the dependency the log names; confirm the loader matches the mods
NoSuchMethodError / NoSuchFieldError
A mod was built for another Minecraft version
Swap it for the build that matches this instance
Mixin apply failed / MixinTransformerError
Switch off the newest mods and add them back one at a time
Unsupported class file major version
Java is older than the game or the mod expects
Use the managed Java in Settings > Java, or install Java 21
Duplicate mods: ...
The same mod exists twice in the folder
Check & repair renames the duplicate; or switch one off
Entrypoint stage 'main' / 'client' failed
A mod failed while starting; the next "Caused by" names it
Read the cause, switch that mod off, report it to the mod author
EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION (often in a driver DLL)
The graphics driver crashed, not Java
Update the GPU driver, turn off overlays, lower graphics settings
A driver crash is worth saying out loud: an access violation inside {0}, {1} or {2} is the GPU driver's own module, and no amount of reinstalling Java will change it.
The Doctor page reads a crash log and writes a numbered list of things to try. It works on the report itself, so you do not have to know which line matters.
From the crash window: press Doctor. The log opens already attached and redacted, and the on-device instructions are ready without an account.
From the website: drop in a {0} or {1} file (up to 2 MB). Uploading starts the analysis by itself.
Paste instead: expand the log editor, paste the text, review it, then press Analyze log. Pasting never sends anything until you press that button.

The result names the mods, dependencies and settings the log points at, and lists the evidence under See the error lines. You can save the instructions as a Markdown file to keep next to the machine you are fixing.
What leaves your computer

Optional AI analysis uses Kilo's free router through Cubeon's server. The excerpt is shared with Kilo and its selected free provider, which may retain or use it. Redaction removes obvious paths and names but cannot catch everything - delete private details before uploading, or paste and review it in the editor instead. If AI is unavailable, the on-device instructions still work.
Clear removes the log and the instructions from the page. The original file on your disk is not touched.
If vanilla launches and a modded instance does not, the mods are the difference. Work in this order:
Press Check & repair in Mods > Installed. It catches duplicates, missing dependencies and version mismatches without disabling anything you did not ask it to.
Switch off what you added last. If the game starts, that mod (or something it needed) was the problem. Report it, or find another build.
Halve the list. Still crashing? Switch off half the mods. Working? The culprit is in the other half. Four or five launches finds almost any single bad mod.
Run the Doctor with the crash report. It reads the "Caused by" chain and usually names the file.

Two failures look like mods but are not: running a pack with a second copy of a library the pack already ships, and installing a mod while the game is open. Both are fixed by the list above, but neither is a bug in the mod.
Render distance first. It is the single biggest setting, and the one people forget they raised.
Shaders second. A heavy shader pack can cost more than everything else combined. Try the "fast" or "potato" preset before you uninstall anything.
Check FPS boost is on. It is the Play-menu switch that installs Sodium and its companions. The benchmarks page shows what it is worth on real hardware.
Memory: enough, not maximum. 4 GB is right for vanilla, 6-8 GB for a pack. Beyond that, the garbage collector does more work for no gain.
Laptops: make sure the game is on the dedicated GPU and the laptop is plugged in. A power-saving profile ignores most of the above.
Close what is behind the game. A browser with 40 tabs is competing for the same memory and GPU.
If it is fine for a minute and then stutters regularly, that is usually memory or world generation, not the launcher. If it is slow from the first second, it is settings.
Close the game before copying or deleting a world. Half-written region files are how worlds actually get damaged.
Try it on the same instance it was made in. A world that was played with mods may refuse to load without them - the log says which block or entity is missing.
Restore a backup. If you made one, this is the moment. Backups shows what Cubeon saves and what it does not.
Do not delete the folder yet. A world that fails to load is often still intact; keep the folder somewhere else while you try to open it, rather than clearing space with it.
Ask on the Discord for a quick answer, or email hamza.457.shahbaz@gmail.com. A report that gets fixed quickly usually has:
your operating system and Cubeon version;
what you did, in order, and what happened instead;
the crash report or the last 30 lines of {0};
whether it also happens on vanilla.
Before you send a log, remove tokens, identity files, private server addresses and anything you would not post publicly. Which log to send lists the files and what is in them.
